SCoUT: Scalable Communication via Utility-Guided Temporal Grouping in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

Manav Vora, Gokul Puthumanaillam, Hiroyasu Tsukamoto, Melkior Ornik

Keywords: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning, Communication Scheduling, Large Scale Multi-Agent Systems.

Abstract

Communication can improve coordination in partially observed multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), but learning when and who to communicate with requires choosing among many possible sender-recipient pairs, and the effect of any single message on future reward is hard to isolate. We introduce SCoUT (Scalable Communication via Utility-guided Temporal grouping), which addresses both these challenges via temporal and agent abstraction within traditional MARL. During training, SCoUT resamples soft agent groups every KK environment steps (macro-steps) via Gumbel-Softmax; these groups are latent clusters that induce an affinity used as a differentiable prior over recipients. Using the same assignments, a group-aware critic predicts values for each agent group and maps them to per-agent baselines through the same soft assignments, reducing critic complexity and variance. Each agent is trained with a three-headed policy: environment action, send decision, and recipient selection. To obtain precise communication learning signals, we derive counterfactual communication advantages by analytically removing each sender’s contribution from the recipient’s aggregated messages. This counterfactual computation enables precise credit assignment for both send and recipient-selection decisions. At execution time, all centralized training components are discarded and only the per-agent policy is run, preserving decentralized execution. Experiments on large-scale benchmarks show that SCoUT learns targeted communication and remains effective in large scenarios, while prior methods degrade as the population grows. Finally, ablations confirm that temporal grouping and counterfactual communication credit are both critical for scalability.

Project website, videos and code: https://scout-comm.github.io/

1 Introduction

Communication is a natural mechanism for coordination in partially observed multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL): exchanging local information or intent can mitigate limited individual views and help synchronize behavior toward a shared objective (Bernstein et al., 2002; Hernandez-Leal et al., 2019; Buşoniu et al., 2008). Accordingly, recent work learns communication protocols and routing decisions end-to-end alongside agent policies, rather than prescribing a fixed topology or hand-designed messages (Niu et al., 2021; Li et al., 2021). Yet scaling learned communication beyond small teams remains difficult, with growing computational cost and training instability as the agent population increases (Li et al., 2021).

A key bottleneck in scaling learned communication is that deciding when and with whom to communicate is inherently combinatorial: at each step, the team implicitly chooses a communication graph over NN agents, yielding 2N⁡(N−1)2^{N(N-1)} possible link patterns. Fully connected architectures avoid explicit routing decisions but require O⁡(N2)O(N^{2}) message exchanges and aggregations per step, which can become costly and inject substantial irrelevant traffic as NN grows (Sukhbaatar et al., 2016; Foerster et al., 2016). Selective communication methods reduce per-step communication and computation by gating or scheduling transmissions (Singh et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2019) or by learning targeted routing with attention (Jiang and Lu, 2018; Das et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2020). However, these approaches are typically trained under centralized training with decentralized execution using actor-critic objectives, where centralized value functions provide learning signals for both environment actions and communication decisions (Lowe et al., 2017; Yu et al., 2022). As the population grows, two challenges often persist at training time: (i) training-time scalability–critics and communication modules must process high-dimensional, multi-agent information; and (ii) credit assignment–attributing downstream returns to specific messages and recipient choices when many communications jointly influence outcomes (Foerster et al., 2018). Empirically, learned-communication results are typically demonstrated at scales of 𝒪⁡(10CLOSE\mathcal{O}(10-OPEN100)100) agents (Li et al., 2025).

To make learned communication feasible for large teams with hundreds of agents, we propose SCoUT (Scalable COmmunication via Utility-guided Temporal grouping), a training framework that introduces temporal and agent abstraction. The core idea is to treat the communication structure as a slowly varying latent variable: every KK environment steps (a macro-step), SCoUT resamples a set of soft agent groups–a differentiable clustering of agents to a small number of latent groups–using differentiable categorical sampling (Jang et al., 2017; Maddison et al., 2017). These group affinities induce a differentiable prior over recipient selection and message aggregation in a one-step-latency mailbox, i.e., a per-agent message buffer of received messages from the previous step. The same group assignments also factor value estimation through a group-aware critic that predicts group-level values and maps them back to per-agent baselines, reducing critic complexity and variance. We train each agent with a three-headed PPO policy (environment action, send, recipient selection) (Schulman et al., 2017; Schulman et al., 2016), and derive counterfactual communication advantages by analytically removing a sender’s contribution from a recipient’s aggregated mailbox, in the spirit of counterfactual baselines for multi-agent credit assignment (Foerster et al., 2018).

Contributions.

  1. (i)

    We introduce a temporally-extended soft-grouping mechanism for MARL communication, that induces a learned distribution over recipients. This mechanism replaces per-step combinatorial link selection over 2N⁡(N−1)2^{N(N-1)} possible directed communication graphs, with structured, differentiable routing guided by group affinities.

  2. (ii)

    We propose a group-aware critic that factors value prediction through soft groups and maps group values back to per-agent baselines, improving the scalability and stability of CTDE training in large populations.

  3. (iii)

    We develop a counterfactual mailbox credit-assignment rule that yields direct learning signals for both sending and recipient selection by analytically removing a sender’s contribution from a recipient’s aggregated messages.

At execution time, SCoUT discards centralized components (group sampler, critic, and counterfactual computations) and runs only the learned per-agent policy, preserving decentralized execution.

We evaluate SCoUT on large-scale cooperative benchmarks from PettingZoo (Terry et al., 2021) and MAgent (Zheng et al., 2018), where it learns targeted communication while scaling to hundreds of agents and outperforming state-of-the-art baselines as population size grows; ablations in Pursuit isolate the impact of temporal grouping and counterfactual credit assignment.

2 Related Work

Foundations and CTDE training.

Partially observed multi-agent decision-making is captured by decentralized control formalisms such as Dec-POMDPs (Bernstein et al., 2002) and by Markov games (Littman, 1994). Deep MARL commonly adopts centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE), using global information to train critics or value decompositions while executing decentralized policies (Lowe et al., 2017; Foerster et al., 2018). Representative CTDE methods include centralized critics (MADDPG) (Lowe et al., 2017), counterfactual actor–critic learning (COMA) (Foerster et al., 2018), and value factorization (VDN/QMIX, QTRAN, QPLEX) (Sunehag et al., 2018; Rashid et al., 2020; Son et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2021); PPO-style CTDE baselines such as MAPPO are also competitive (Schulman et al., 2017; Yu et al., 2022). As the number of agents grows, however, centralized critics can become a bottleneck: they must summarize high-dimensional interactions and provide low-variance learning signals. SCoUT addresses this by factoring value estimation through soft groups and mapping group values to per-agent baselines.

Learned communication in MARL.

A long line of work learns differentiable communication end-to-end, enabling agents to exchange messages that improve coordination under partial observability. CommNet aggregates broadcast-style continuous messages (Sukhbaatar et al., 2016), while DIAL/RIAL learn communication alongside decentralized policies with differentiable and discrete channels (Foerster et al., 2016). For large populations, dense communication becomes inefficient and noisy, and message utility is difficult to disentangle. Selective schemes reduce transmissions by learning when to communicate (IC3Net) (Singh et al., 2019) or scheduling a subset of speakers under bandwidth constraints (Kim et al., 2019). Yet these methods typically re-decide communication each step and rely on centralized training signals, making credit assignment for communication increasingly challenging at scale. To alleviate this scalability issue, SCoUT introduces temporal abstraction via soft groups that persist for KK steps and a counterfactual mailbox signal that efficiently trains both sending and recipient selection.

Targeted routing, attention, and structure.

Beyond “speak or stay silent,” targeted routing methods learn with whom to communicate. ATOC forms temporary coordination groups via attention (Jiang and Lu, 2018), TarMAC learns attention-based addressing (Das et al., 2019), and G2ANet models relations with multi-stage attention (Liu et al., 2020); ToM2C incorporates Theory-of-Mind-style inference (Wang et al., 2022). These approaches provide richer structure than broadcasting but often evaluate routing over many potential recipients and can be expensive or unstable when recomputed at every step for large NN. In parallel, topology-design approaches advocate fixed global structures; for example, ExpoComm leverages exponential-graph topologies for small-diameter dissemination (Li et al., 2025). SCoUT sits between these directions by learning a task-adaptive grouping structure that changes slowly over time and acts as a structured bias over recipient selection, without fixed topology or per-step global rerouting.

Scalability and many-agent benchmarks.

Scaling MARL has also been pursued via mean-field approximations that replace many-body interactions with aggregate effects (Yang et al., 2018). Standardized benchmarks enable evaluation across regimes, including SMAC (Samvelyan et al., 2019) and many-agent gridworlds in MAgent (Zheng et al., 2018). SCoUT is motivated by large finite populations with heterogeneous local observations and structured coordination needs, where dense communication and monolithic critics become impractical and credit assignment for communication decisions is particularly acute.

3 Problem Setting

We consider cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning under partial observability, modeled as a decentralized partially observable Markov decision process (Dec-POMDP) (Bernstein et al., 2002). A Dec-POMDP is defined by ⟨𝒮,{𝒜i}i=1N,𝒫,r,{𝒪i}i=1N,𝒵,γ⟩\langle\mathcal{S},\{\mathcal{A}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N},\mathcal{P},r,\{\mathcal{O}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N},\mathcal{Z},\gamma\rangle, where st∈𝒮s_{t}\in\mathcal{S} is the environment state, each agent i∈{1,…,N}i\in\{1,\dots,N\} selects an environment action ati∈𝒜ia_{t}^{i}\in\mathcal{A}_{i}, the transition kernel is 𝒫⁡(st+1∣st,at1,…,atN)\mathcal{P}(s_{t+1}\mid s_{t},a_{t}^{1},\dots,a_{t}^{N}), and all agents share a cooperative reward r⁡(st,at1,…,atN)r(s_{t},a_{t}^{1},\dots,a_{t}^{N}) with discount factor γ∈(0,1)\gamma\in(0,1). Each agent receives a local observation oti∈𝒪io_{t}^{i}\in\mathcal{O}_{i} emitted by 𝒵⁡(ot1,…,otN∣st)\mathcal{Z}(o_{t}^{1},\dots,o_{t}^{N}\mid s_{t}) and acts based on its local history hti=(o1:ti,a1:t−1i)h_{t}^{i}=(o_{1:t}^{i},a_{1:t-1}^{i}).

Communication interface.

In addition to environment actions, agents may communicate over a directed, point-to-point channel. At time tt, agent ii chooses (i) a binary send decision cti∈{0,1}c_{t}^{i}\in\{0,1\}, (ii) if cti=1c_{t}^{i}=1, a recipient index ρti∈{1,…,N}\rho_{t}^{i}\in\{1,\dots,N\}, and (iii) a message vector xti∈𝒳⊆ℝdx_{t}^{i}\in\mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} with fixed dimension dd. We assume a synchronous one-step latency: messages sent at time tt are available to recipients at time t+1t{+}1. Since a recipient may receive multiple messages in the same step, we represent its incoming communication by a fixed-dimensional mailbox vector mt+1j∈ℝdmm_{t+1}^{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{m}} obtained via an aggregation operator

mt+1j=g({xti:cti=1,ρti=j}),m_{t+1}^{j}\;=\;g\!\left(\{x_{t}^{i}:\;c_{t}^{i}=1,\ \rho_{t}^{i}=j\}\right),

where gg maps a multiset of incoming messages to a single vector and mt+1j=𝟎m_{t+1}^{j}=\mathbf{0} if no messages are addressed to jj.

Policies and objective.

A stochastic decentralized policy for agent ii is a conditional distribution over its decisions given its local information, i.e., πi(⋅∣hti,mti)\pi^{i}(\cdot\mid h_{t}^{i},m_{t}^{i}). We assume parameter sharing and use a single policy πθ\pi_{\theta} for all agents (Christianos et al., 2021; Terry et al., 2020):

(ati,cti,xti,ρti)∼πθ(⋅∣hti,mti),∀i∈{1,…,N}.(a_{t}^{i},c_{t}^{i},x_{t}^{i},\rho_{t}^{i})\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid h_{t}^{i},m_{t}^{i}),\qquad\forall i\in\{1,\dots,N\}.

This induces a joint policy that factorizes across agents conditioned on their local inputs,

𝝅θ(𝐚t,𝐜t,𝐱t,𝝆t∣𝐡t,𝐦t)=∏i=1Nπθ(ati,cti,xti,ρti∣hti,mti).\boldsymbol{\pi}_{\theta}(\mathbf{a}_{t},\mathbf{c}_{t},\mathbf{x}_{t},\boldsymbol{\rho}_{t}\mid\mathbf{h}_{t},\mathbf{m}_{t})=\prod_{i=1}^{N}\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}^{i},c_{t}^{i},x_{t}^{i},\rho_{t}^{i}\mid h_{t}^{i},m_{t}^{i}).

Our goal is to maximize the expected discounted team return

J⁡(𝝅θ)=𝔼𝝅θ​[∑t=0∞γt​r​(st,at1,…,atN)].J(\boldsymbol{\pi}_{\theta})=\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\pi}_{\theta}}\!\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}\,r(s_{t},a_{t}^{1},\dots,a_{t}^{N})\right]. (1)

Learning setup (CTDE).

We adopt centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE): at execution time, each agent acts using only (hti,mti)(h_{t}^{i},m_{t}^{i}), while during training we may leverage additional global information (which in our case is the global state) to learn critics or auxiliary components (Lowe et al., 2017; Foerster et al., 2018).

4 SCoUT

We now describe our framework for scalable, utility-guided communication in cooperative MARL. SCoUT (i) introduces a slowly varying latent communication structure via soft grouping rather than re-deciding a dense communication graph at every step, (ii) uses this structure to simplify and factor value estimation through a group-aware critic, and (iii) trains targeted communication decisions, including the binary send action cti∈{0,1}c_{t}^{i}\in\{0,1\} and recipient choice ρti\rho_{t}^{i}, using counterfactual advantages that attribute utility to individual messages. Figure 1 provides a training forward-pass overview of SCoUT, highlighting the macro-step grouping and the per-step three-headed communication policy.

4.1 Agent backbone and descriptors

Each agent runs a shared recurrent backbone to maintain memory under partial observability. Let φ⁡(⋅)\varphi(\cdot) embed the concatenated local observation and mailbox input. We maintain an internal recurrent state utiu_{t}^{i} with a GRU (Cho et al., 2014):

uti=GRU⁡(φ⁡([oti,mti]),ut−1i).u_{t}^{i}=\mathrm{GRU}\!\bigl(\varphi([o_{t}^{i},\,m_{t}^{i}]),\,u_{t-1}^{i}\bigr).

From utiu_{t}^{i} we compute a lightweight descriptor via two learned projections: (i) a grouping descriptor ztgrp,iz_{t}^{\mathrm{grp},i}, evaluated only every KK steps (at macro-step boundaries), and (ii) a message descriptor ztmsg,iz_{t}^{\mathrm{msg},i}, used as message content when the agent transmits. All representation parameters are trained end-to-end through gradients from the policy and value objectives, as well as the grouping and communication components introduced below.

4.2 Temporal soft grouping and affinity prior

A central difficulty in large-team communication is that choosing a directed communication pattern at every step introduces many coupled discrete decisions; with sparse/delayed rewards, this can lead to high-variance gradients and brittle credit assignment. SCoUT mitigates this by introducing a slowly varying latent structure: every macro-step bb (every KK primitive steps), we sample soft groups that act as (i) a coarse, persistent notion of communication neighborhoods and (ii) a reusable structure for downstream components (see the top panel of Figure 1).

Let tbt_{b} denote the first primitive step of macro-step bb. We assign each agent ii to one of M≪NM\ll N latent groups using its grouping descriptor ztbgrp,iz_{t_{b}}^{\mathrm{grp},i} and a set of learnable group prototypes {pg}g=1M\{p_{g}\}_{g=1}^{M}. Intuitively, prototypes serve as anchor points, akin to soft kk-means centroids. We compute assignment logits via cosine similarity:

ℓtbi,g=α⋅⟨ztbgrp,i,pg⟩‖ztbgrp,i‖​‖pg‖,g∈{1,…,M},\ell_{t_{b}}^{i,g}=\alpha\cdot\frac{\langle z_{t_{b}}^{\mathrm{grp},i},\,p_{g}\rangle}{\|z_{t_{b}}^{\mathrm{grp},i}\|\,\|p_{g}\|},\qquad g\in\{1,\dots,M\},

where α>0\alpha>0 is a learnable scale. We then sample soft assignments with the Gumbel–Softmax reparameterization (Jang et al., 2017; Maddison et al., 2017):

Ytbi,g=softmax​(ℓtbi,⋅+ϵi,⋅τ)g,ϵi,g∼Gumbel⁡(0,1),Y_{t_{b}}^{i,g}=\mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{\ell_{t_{b}}^{i,\cdot}+\epsilon^{i,\cdot}}{\tau}\right)_{g},\quad\epsilon^{i,g}\sim\mathrm{Gumbel}(0,1),

with temperature τ\tau, yielding Ytb∈ℝN×MY_{t_{b}}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times M}. Following common practice in differentiable pooling (Ying et al., 2018), we form an affinity matrix

Gtb=Ytb​Ytb⊤∈ℝN×N.G_{t_{b}}\;=\;Y_{t_{b}}Y_{t_{b}}^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}.

where Gtbi​jG_{t_{b}}^{ij} is large when agents ii and jj are assigned to similar groups.This affinity is held fixed for the entire macro-step and serves as a differentiable prior over communication partners.

Grouping objective.

Because grouping is a stochastic latent decision, we optimize it with a score-function objective (Williams, 1992) using a macro-step advantage signal. Let Pτi,g=softmax​(ℓtbi,⋅/τ)gP_{\tau}^{i,g}=\mathrm{softmax}(\ell_{t_{b}}^{i,\cdot}/\tau)_{g} denote the assignment probabilities and let Abgrp,iA_{b}^{\mathrm{grp},i} denote the macro-step advantage produced by the group-aware critic (Section 4.4). We minimize

ℒgrp=ℒgrpPG+λbal​ℒgrpbal+λent​ℒgrpent+λedge​ℒgrpedge,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{grp}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{grp}}^{\mathrm{PG}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{bal}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{grp}}^{\mathrm{bal}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{ent}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{grp}}^{\mathrm{ent}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{edge}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{grp}}^{\mathrm{edge}},

where λbal,λent,λedge≥0\lambda_{\mathrm{bal}},\lambda_{\mathrm{ent}},\lambda_{\mathrm{edge}}\geq 0 are user-chosen coefficients controlling the strength of each regularizer. The policy-gradient term is

ℒgrpPG=−∑b∑i=1NAbgrp,i∑g=1MYtbi,glogPτi,g,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{grp}}^{\mathrm{PG}}=-\sum_{b}\sum_{i=1}^{N}A_{b}^{\mathrm{grp},i}\,\sum_{g=1}^{M}Y_{t_{b}}^{i,g}\,\log P_{\tau}^{i,g},

which applies the score-function weight to the sampled assignment. We additionally regularize against degenerate or premature collapse:

ℒgrpbal\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{grp}}^{\mathrm{bal}} =‖1N​∑i=1NPτi−1M​𝟏‖22,\displaystyle=\left\|\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}P_{\tau}^{i}-\frac{1}{M}\mathbf{1}\right\|_{2}^{2}, ℒgrpent\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{grp}}^{\mathrm{ent}} =−1N∑i=1NH(Pτi),\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}H(P_{\tau}^{i}),

where ℒgrpbal\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{grp}}^{\mathrm{bal}} encourages roughly balanced group usage and ℒgrpent\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{grp}}^{\mathrm{ent}} encourages exploration early in training. Finally, ℒgrpedge\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{grp}}^{\mathrm{edge}} encourages the learned affinity GtbG_{t_{b}} to place higher weight on agent pairs whose communication is predicted to be useful under our learned pairwise utility signal (Section 4.5).

4.3 Three-headed policy and mailbox communication

Each agent uses a shared policy πθ(⋅∣uti)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid u_{t}^{i}) with three heads: (i) an environment-action head, (ii) a binary send head cti∈{0,1}c_{t}^{i}\in\{0,1\}, and (iii) a recipient head over ρti∈{1,…,N}\rho_{t}^{i}\in\{1,\dots,N\}. The backbone produces two descriptors (Section 4.1): ztmsg,i∈ℝdz_{t}^{\mathrm{msg},i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, used as the agent’s message representation, and ztbgrp,iz_{t_{b}}^{\mathrm{grp},i}, used for grouping at macro-step boundaries. When agent ii sends (cti=1c_{t}^{i}=1), it transmits the message vector xti≜ztmsg,i∈ℝdx_{t}^{i}\;\triangleq\;z_{t}^{\mathrm{msg},i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, and samples a recipient ρti\rho_{t}^{i} from the recipient head (see the bottom panel of Figure 1).

Recipient bias from group affinity.

Let ϕtrecv,i∈ℝN\phi_{t}^{\mathrm{recv},i}\in\mathbb{R}^{N} denote the recipient logits produced by agent ii’s policy head at time tt. To encourage within-group communication without hard constraints, we add a macro-step-dependent log-bias derived from the affinity matrix GtbG_{t_{b}}:

ϕ~trecv,i​(j)=ϕtrecv,i​(j)+log⁡(Gtbi​j+ε),j∈{1,…,N},\tilde{\phi}_{t}^{\mathrm{recv},i}(j)=\phi_{t}^{\mathrm{recv},i}(j)+\log\!\bigl(G_{t_{b}}^{ij}+\varepsilon\bigr),\quad j\in\{1,\dots,N\},

where tbt_{b} is the macro-step containing tt and ε>0\varepsilon>0 is a small constant. We then sample ρti\rho_{t}^{i} from softmax⁡(ϕ~trecv,i)\mathrm{softmax}(\tilde{\phi}_{t}^{\mathrm{recv},i}).

Mailbox aggregation (choice of gg).

As defined in Section 3, a recipient may receive a variable number of incoming messages; we therefore map the multiset of received message vectors to a fixed-dimensional mailbox mt+1jm_{t+1}^{j} using an aggregation operator g⁡(⋅)g(\cdot). This provides a permutation-invariant, fixed-size input to the policy at the next step. In our implementation we choose a simple parameter-free scaled dot-product attention rule (Vaswani et al., 2017):

mt+1j=∑i:ρti=jwi​jxti,wi​j=exp⁡(⟨xtj,xti⟩/d)∑i′:ρti′=jexp(⟨xtj,xti′⟩/d),\displaystyle m_{t+1}^{j}=\sum_{i:\,\rho_{t}^{i}=j}w_{ij}\,x_{t}^{i},\quad w_{ij}=\frac{\exp\!\bigl(\langle x_{t}^{j},x_{t}^{i}\rangle/\sqrt{d}\bigr)}{\sum\limits_{i^{\prime}:\,\rho_{t}^{i^{\prime}}=j}\exp\!\bigl(\langle x_{t}^{j},x_{t}^{i^{\prime}}\rangle/\sqrt{d}\bigr)}, (2)

where dd is the message dimension. Intuitively, the recipient’s own message descriptor xtjx_{t}^{j} acts as a query that weights incoming message descriptors which act as keys and values.

4.4 Group-aware critic and grouping advantage

Group-aware critic.

Under CTDE, we learn a centralized value function that estimates expected discounted team return from the global state. To reduce output complexity for large populations, SCoUT predicts values at the group level and converts them into per-agent value baselines, used for advantage estimation, using the soft assignments. Concretely, given sts_{t}, the critic outputs 𝐯t=[vt1,…,vtM]⊤=Vψ​(st)∈ℝM\mathbf{v}_{t}=[v_{t}^{1},\dots,v_{t}^{M}]^{\top}=V_{\psi}(s_{t})\in\mathbb{R}^{M}, and the per-agent baseline is the assignment-weighted mixture

Vti=∑g=1MPτi,g​vtg=(Pτ​𝐯t)i.V_{t}^{i}=\sum_{g=1}^{M}P_{\tau}^{i,g}\,v_{t}^{g}=\bigl(P_{\tau}\mathbf{v}_{t}\bigr)_{i}.

We train VψV_{\psi} with the standard PPO/GAE value regression objective ℒV\mathcal{L}_{V}: we form bootstrapped targets from GAE (Schulman et al., 2016) and minimize a squared-error loss (Schulman et al., 2017).

Grouping advantage.

At each macro-step boundary tbt_{b}, we derive an advantage signal for the grouping module by comparing the predicted per-agent value under the learned assignment to a permutation baseline. Let σ\sigma be a random permutation of {1,…,M}\{1,\dots,M\} and define the permuted group-value vector (𝐯tbσ)g≜𝐯tb,σ⁡(g)(\mathbf{v}_{t_{b}}^{\sigma})_{g}\triangleq\mathbf{v}_{t_{b},\sigma(g)}. We set

Abgrp,i=(Pτ​𝐯tb)i⏟value under learned grouping−(Pτ​𝐯tbσ)i⏟permutation baseline.A_{b}^{\mathrm{grp},i}=\underbrace{\bigl(P_{\tau}\mathbf{v}_{t_{b}}\bigr)_{i}}_{\text{value under learned grouping}}-\underbrace{\bigl(P_{\tau}\mathbf{v}_{t_{b}}^{\sigma}\bigr)_{i}}_{\text{permutation baseline}}.

Subtracting the second term acts as a REINFORCE-style baseline. It preserves the scale of predicted values while being independent of the particular group labeling, and thus, reduces gradient variance for learning the grouping distribution (Williams, 1992; Greensmith et al., 2004).

4.5 Communication critic and counterfactual mailbox credit assignment

A core difficulty in learned communication is credit assignment: multiple simultaneous messages can jointly influence future rewards. SCoUT learns an auxiliary communication critic with two heads: (i) a message-conditioned value head VωmsgV_{\omega}^{\mathrm{msg}} for recipient evaluation, and (ii) a pairwise utility head QωQ_{\omega} for sender–recipient utilities. We train this critic by minimizing squared one-step Temporal Difference (TD) errors (Sutton, 1988) over a batch of TT primitive steps per update, using Polyak averaging (Polyak and Juditsky, 1992; Lillicrap et al., 2016).

Counterfactual send advantage.

For a sender ii that addressed recipient j=ρtij=\rho_{t}^{i}, we compute a counterfactual mailbox that removes ii’s contribution while keeping all other incoming messages fixed, following the counterfactual credit assignment paradigm discussed in Foerster et al. (2018). For a sender ii that addressed recipient j=ρtij=\rho_{t}^{i}, let mt+1j=g({xti′:cti′=1,ρti′=j})m_{t+1}^{j}=g(\{x_{t}^{i^{\prime}}:\,c_{t}^{i^{\prime}}=1,\ \rho_{t}^{i^{\prime}}=j\}), as defined in Section 3. We define the leave-one-out counterfactual mailbox by removing ii’s message and re-applying the same aggregator mt+1j∖i=g({xti′:cti′=1,ρti′=j,i′≠i}).m_{t+1}^{j\setminus i}=g\!\left(\{x_{t}^{i^{\prime}}:\,c_{t}^{i^{\prime}}=1,\ \rho_{t}^{i^{\prime}}=j,\ i^{\prime}\neq i\}\right). In our implementation, where gg is the parameter-free attention rule in (2), this reduces to a normalized leave-one-out attention aggregate:

mt+1j∖i=∑i′∈𝒮t​(j)∖{i}wi′​j∑k∈𝒮t​(j)∖{i}wk​j​xti′.m_{t+1}^{j\setminus i}=\sum_{i^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S}_{t}(j)\setminus\{i\}}\frac{w_{i^{\prime}j}}{\sum_{k\in\mathcal{S}_{t}(j)\setminus\{i\}}w_{kj}}\;x_{t}^{i^{\prime}}.

Subsequently, we define the send advantage as

Atsend,i=Vωmsg​(st+1,ft+1j​(mt+1j))−Vωmsg​(st+1,ft+1j​(mt+1j∖i)),A_{t}^{\mathrm{send},i}=V_{\omega}^{\mathrm{msg}}\!\bigl(s_{t+1},\,f_{t+1}^{j}(m_{t+1}^{j})\bigr)-V_{\omega}^{\mathrm{msg}}\!\bigl(s_{t+1},\,f_{t+1}^{j}(m_{t+1}^{j\setminus i})\bigr),

where ft+1j​(⋅)f_{t+1}^{j}(\cdot) denotes the recipient feature construction with the specified mailbox input.

Recipient advantage and edge-utility alignment.

Let the pairwise utility matrix at time tt be

Uti​j:=Qω​(st+1,fti,ft+1j),U_{t}^{ij}:=Q_{\omega}\!\bigl(s_{t+1},\,f_{t}^{i},\,f_{t+1}^{j}\bigr),

for valid sender-recipient pairs (i,j)(i,j). For a sender ii with chosen recipient ρti\rho_{t}^{i}, we form a centered recipient advantage

Atrecv,i=Uti​ρti−1|ℛti|​∑j∈ℛtiUti​j,A_{t}^{\mathrm{recv},i}=U_{t}^{i\rho_{t}^{i}}-\frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}_{t}^{i}|}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{R}_{t}^{i}}U_{t}^{ij},

where ℛti\mathcal{R}_{t}^{i} is the set of possible recipients for ii. To align grouping with communication utility, we define G~tbi,⋅\tilde{G}_{t_{b}}^{i,\cdot} and U~tbi,⋅\tilde{U}_{t_{b}}^{i,\cdot} as row-centered and ℓ2\ell_{2}-normalized versions of the affinity and utility rows respectively, and set

ℒgrpedge=−1N∑i=1N⟨G~tbi,⋅,U~tbi,⋅⟩‖G~tbi,⋅‖​‖U~tbi,⋅‖.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{grp}}^{\mathrm{edge}}=-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{\langle\tilde{G}_{t_{b}}^{i,\cdot},\,\tilde{U}_{t_{b}}^{i,\cdot}\rangle}{\|\tilde{G}_{t_{b}}^{i,\cdot}\|\,\|\tilde{U}_{t_{b}}^{i,\cdot}\|}.

This is akin to computing cosine similarity between row vectors of two matrices (Brockmeier and others, 2017) and encourages groups to be communication-consistent: agents are grouped together when the learned utility predicts that they are useful communication partners, and pushed apart otherwise.

4.6 Overall optimization and decentralized execution

We train the three-headed policy with PPO (Schulman et al., 2017), using (i) standard GAE advantages for environment actions (Schulman et al., 2016) and (ii) the communication advantages Atsend,iA_{t}^{\mathrm{send},i} and Atrecv,iA_{t}^{\mathrm{recv},i} above for the send and recipient heads. Let ℒPPOenv,ℒPPOsend,ℒPPOrecv\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PPO}}^{\mathrm{env}},\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PPO}}^{\mathrm{send}},\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PPO}}^{\mathrm{recv}} denote the standard clipped PPO surrogates for each head with their corresponding advantages. The full objective combines policy, environment critic, communication critic, and grouping losses:

ℒ=ℒPPOenv+ℒPPOsend+ℒPPOrecv+cV​ℒV+cω​ℒω+cgrp​ℒgrp,\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PPO}}^{\mathrm{env}}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PPO}}^{\mathrm{send}}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PPO}}^{\mathrm{recv}}+c_{V}\mathcal{L}_{V}+c_{\omega}\mathcal{L}_{\omega}+c_{\mathrm{grp}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{grp}},

where ℒω\mathcal{L}_{\omega} denotes the communication critic loss described in Section 4.5. The coefficients cV,cω,cgrp≥0c_{V},c_{\omega},c_{\mathrm{grp}}\geq 0 are user-chosen scalar weights that trade off the auxiliary losses against the PPO policy losses; we treat them as hyperparameters. At test time, SCoUT discards centralized training components and executes only the shared decentralized policy per agent.

5 Experiments

We evaluate SCoUT on two large-population multi-agent benchmarks with two goals: (i) show that SCoUT can be trained directly at hundreds of agents while retaining strong coordination; and (ii) isolate which design choices drive these gains.

5.1 Benchmarks

MAgent Battle.

We consider the Battle scenario in MAgent (Zheng et al., 2018), a competitive two-team gridworld where each team must coordinate to eliminate the opposing team under a fixed episode horizon. At each step, each agent chooses to either move or attack; attacks reduce the target’s health, and agents are eliminated when their health reaches zero (additional details for Battle can be found in Appendix A.1). We evaluate four population scales: 20v20, 64v64, 81v81, and 100v100. Notably, prior structured-communication results on this benchmark are typically reported up to 64v64; our 81v81 and 100v100 settings explicitly stress-test scalability beyond that regime.

Pursuit (SISL).

We also evaluate on Pursuit from the PettingZoo SISL suite (Terry et al., 2021), consisting of P pursuers and E evaders (E<<P). An evader is captured when all free adjacent cells around it are occupied by pursuers; thus the required number of pursuers is 4 in open space, 3 along walls/obstacles, and 2 in corners (additional details for Pursuit can be found in Appendix A.2). We use Pursuit primarily for targeted ablations to understand which components of SCoUT are necessary for strong coordination. We evaluate five scales: 20P-8E, 40P-16E, 60P-24E, 80P-32E, and 100P-40E. Unlike the default Pursuit configuration (8 pursuers, 30 evaders) (Terry et al., 2021; Gerstgrasser et al., 2023), we study regimes with E<PE<P to stress-test scalability with respect to the number of learning agents while keeping capture milestones informative under a fixed 500-step horizon.

Across all benchmarks, we use a fixed macro-step length K=10K{=}10 and set the number of groups by a simple scale-dependent rule. For Battle: M=⌊N⌋M=\lfloor\sqrt{N}\rfloor with NN agents per team and for Pursuit: M=⌊E/2⌋M=\lfloor E/2\rfloor with EE evaders. Appendix B summarizes all the hyperparameters used in the experiments and Appendix D presents a sensitivity study for the choice of MM and KK.

Compute. All experiments were run on a machine with an NVIDIA L40 GPU and an AMD CPU (32 cores @ 4.1 GHz).

5.2 Scalable competitive coordination on MAgent Battle

Setup and claim under test.

This experiment evaluates whether SCoUT maintains robust and decisive competitive coordination as population size grows. Unlike previous work emphasizing zero-shot transfer from small-NN training, we train each method directly at the target scale (up to 100v100), stressing optimization stability in the large-instance regime. All methods are trained for 4M steps.

Baselines.

We compare against one non-communication baseline and several learned-communication baselines:

  1. (i)

    Independent deep Q-learning (IDQN)  (Rashid et al., 2020; Mnih and others, 2015), where each agent learns from its local observation without explicit message exchange.

  2. (ii)

    CommFormer (Hu et al., 2024) uses a transformer-style message encoder with attention over other agents’ communication tokens, enabling content-based routing and richer interaction modeling compared to fixed-topology schemes. We include it as a representative attention-based learned-communication baseline.

  3. (iii)

    ExpoComm (Li et al., 2025), designed for many-agent communication via exponential-topology neighborhoods. We evaluate Peer-n=7n{=}7 (time-varying neighborhood) and Static-n=7n{=}7 (fixed neighborhood) under the same per-agent recipient budget.

Metrics and evaluation protocol.

We evaluate each trained policy on 20 independent evaluation seeds per setting. We report: (i) win rate (% episodes where the red team finishes with more agents alive than the blue team); (ii) elimination rate (% blue eliminated, i.e., blue kills divided by NN); and (iii) decisiveness via time-to-milestone: TT50\mathrm{TT}_{50} / TT75\mathrm{TT}_{75} = steps to reach 50% / 75% blue elimination (horizon=200). We additionally report reach rates R50/R75, the % of evaluation episodes that reach each milestone within the horizon. We report TTk\mathrm{TT}_{k} only when Rk≥50%{}_{k}\geq 50\% (otherwise, N/A). Furthermore, we plot training curves (episode return vs. environment steps; Figure 2) to assess optimization stability and sample efficiency when training directly at each target scale. Finally, to characterize how learned communication aligns with the discovered interaction structure, we report the in-group message fraction across all scales in Appendix C.3(Table 8). We also present qualitative rollouts for the 100v100 scenario (Appendix C.1).

Results and discussion.

Table 1 and Figure 2 show two consistent patterns11 1 CommFormer training curves are truncated for larger scales: 81v81 reached ≈\approx50% of the planned 4M steps while 100v100 reached ≈\approx35% (both after 6 days, ∼\sim4×\times the wall-clock budget used for SCoUT).. (1) SCoUT trains reliably across all scales and is highly repeatable. SCoUT achieves 100% win rate for all NN and sustains near-complete elimination (95–99%), with elimination and milestone times exhibiting very low variance across 20 evaluation seeds. Training is similarly stable: across all four scales, SCoUT shows a clear improvement phase followed by stable convergence with substantially less across-seed dispersion than the baselines (Figure 2); notably, this stability persists even at the largest populations (81v81 and 100v100), where SCoUT converges smoothly and quickly compared to the baselines. At the other end of the spectrum (20v20), SCoUT still learns reliably and significantly outperforms the baselines, while ExpoComm is consistently poor and shows no sustained learning progress. Across scales, the static-topology variant underperforms its adaptive counterpart, suggesting that fixed neighborhoods are overly restrictive in dynamic combat where effective coordination partners shift over time. (2) SCoUT converts wins into decisive elimination more consistently and more quickly. At larger NN, ExpoComm baselines can achieve high win rate, but they often leave substantial opponent mass and fail to reach 75% elimination within the horizon; baseline milestone reach rates degrade with scale, indicating that many winning episodes do not consistently translate advantage into high-elimination outcomes. Even when milestones are reached, SCoUT attains them substantially faster (Table 1), consistent with its smoother and more stable learning dynamics (Figure 2). Notably, it is also the only method with R50=R75=100%{}_{50}{=}\text{R}_{75}{=}100\% at every scale, confirming consistently decisive elimination rather than occasional fast wins.

5.3 Ablations on Pursuit

Setup and claim under test.

We use Pursuit to isolate which ingredients of SCoUT drive scalable multi-agent coordination in cooperative capture. All methods are trained directly at each target scale for 4M steps.

Variants and baseline.

We compare the full method against targeted removals and a scalable-communication baseline:

  1. (i)

    SCoUT: learned grouping + group-aware critic + counterfactual communication advantages.

  2. (ii)

    w/o counterfactual: removes the counterfactual decomposition for communication decisions (uses standard Generalized Advantage Estimation (Schulman et al., 2016)).

  3. (iii)

    w/o grouping: removes learned grouping; consequently, the group-aware critic is disabled.

  4. (iv)

    ExpoComm (Peer-n=7n{=}7): same learned communication baseline as Section 5.2.

Metrics and evaluation protocol.

We evaluate each trained policy on 20 independent evaluation seeds per setting. We report: (i) Catch% (fraction of evaders captured); (ii) Done% (% episodes capturing all evaders); and (iii) decisiveness using the same milestone metrics as in Section 5.2: R50/R75 (milestone reach rate) and TT50/TT75\mathrm{TT}_{50}/\mathrm{TT}_{75} (time-to-milestone), but with milestones defined over the capture fraction rather than elimination. Furthermore, we visualize scaling trends with Catch% and TT50\mathrm{TT}_{50} vs. population size (Figure 3). Finally, similar to battle, we also report the in-group message fraction for Pursuit in Appendix C.3 (Table 8) along with qualitative rollouts for 100P-40E (Appendix C.2).

Results and discussion.

Table 2 and Figure 3 reveal two consistent patterns. (1) Full SCoUT scales with high capture and reliable milestone reach. Across all five scales, SCoUT maintains high Catch% with R50=100%{}_{50}{=}100\%, meaning every evaluation episode reaches 50% capture within 500 steps. It also reaches 75% capture reliably at moderate and large scales, with consistently small milestone times and stable across-seed error bars (Figure 3). We report Done% as full capture within the fixed 500-step horizon; Done% naturally decreases with scale (often to 0%) because the number of evaders increases while full capture requires simultaneously surrounding every remaining evader, making complete capture within 500 steps increasingly unlikely even when partial coordinated capture is strong. (2) Isolation experiments show that counterfactual credit and temporal grouping drive scalability. Removing counterfactual advantages causes an abrupt scaling failure: beyond 20P-8E, Catch% collapses and becomes highly variable, and milestone reach drops sharply–R50 falls to 15-20% for 40P-16E/60P-24E and 5% for 80P-32E), making TT50\mathrm{TT}_{50}/TT75\mathrm{TT}_{75} undefined. At 100P-40E it only partially recovers to R50=55%{}_{50}{=}55\% while still failing to reach 75% reliably. Removing grouping is similarly brittle at scale: Catch% drops to 10-41% for 40P-16E through 100P-40E, with R50≤20%{}_{50}\leq 20\% and R75=0%{}_{75}{=}0\% throughout these larger scenarios, indicating persistent failure to form effective capture coalitions. Together, these ablations support the conclusion that SCoUT’s counterfactual communication learning and temporal grouping are both necessary to sustain high capture and early milestone attainment as the population grows.

6 Conclusion

Scaling learned communication to large teams is difficult because sender-receiver interactions grow combinatorially and message-level credit becomes noisy. We presented SCoUT, an approach which makes communication scalable by learning a slowly-varying latent interaction structure: it resamples soft groups at a macro-step timescale, uses the resulting affinities as a differentiable prior over recipients, and reuses the same structure in a group-aware critic for tractable value learning at large NN. SCoUT further introduces a counterfactual mailbox mechanism that isolates each sender’s marginal contribution to a recipient’s aggregated message, yielding fine-grained learning signals for both sending and recipient selection. Across large-population benchmarks, SCoUT trains directly at target scale and maintains strong, reliable coordination as NN grows. In MAgent Battle, it achieves perfect win rate with near-complete elimination and consistently early milestones, while state-of-the-art baselines are less decisive and less reliable. In Pursuit, SCoUT sustains high capture with early milestones across scales. Ablations confirm that temporal grouping and counterfactual communication credit are both necessary: removing either causes sharp drops in performance at moderate and large scales.

Limitations and future work.

SCoUT adds training-time structure, in particular the macro-step KK and number of groups MM, which we currently set as fixed hyperparameters. Although one setting worked well across our benchmarks, performance can depend on how well KK matches the interaction timescale and MM matches agent behavior heterogeneity. In addition, our leave-one-out mailbox counterfactual provides clean marginal credit for senders under a fixed aggregation rule, but does not capture multi-message interaction effects. Future work includes adapting KK and MM online using signals like recipient entropy or utility drift, extending credit assignment to model message interactions, and evaluating SCoUT under continuous control, heterogeneity, and explicit communication/energy budgets.

Appendix A Environment Details

A.1 MAgent Battle (battle_v3)

Map size to population scale.

In MAgent Battle, the population scale is determined by the (square) map size. For a map of size S×SS\times S, the environment spawns NN agents per team as listed in Table 3 (e.g., S=40⇒64S{=}40\Rightarrow 64 vs 6464).

Agent dynamics and interaction radii.

Each agent occupies one grid cell (1×11{\times}1), has health hp=10\texttt{hp}=10, health recovery rate step_recover=0.1\texttt{step\_recover}=0.1, speed speed=2\texttt{speed}=2, view radius view_range=CircleRange​(3)\texttt{view\_range}=\texttt{CircleRange}(3), attack radius attack_range=CircleRange​(1.5)\texttt{attack\_range}=\texttt{CircleRange}(1.5), and attack damage damage=2\texttt{damage}=2.

Rewards.

The environment provides the following default shaping terms: step reward step_reward=−0.005\texttt{step\_reward}=-0.005, death penalty dead_penalty=−0.1\texttt{dead\_penalty}=-0.1, attack penalty attack_penalty=−0.1\texttt{attack\_penalty}=-0.1, and an additional reward of attack_opponent_reward=0.2\texttt{attack\_opponent\_reward}=0.2 for each successful attack event. In addition, agents receive a kill reward kill_reward=5\texttt{kill\_reward}=5 upon eliminating an opponent. Episodes run until all blue agents are killed or for at most max_cycles=200\texttt{max\_cycles}=200 steps.

Controlled team and opponent policy.

In all Battle experiments, we control the red team, while the blue team acts as an opponent using a pretrained IDQN policy, following the same evaluation protocol used by Li et al. (2025).

Spawn layout.

At reset, each team is initialized as a dense square formation on opposite sides of the map. Let SS be the map size. The environment sets init_num=0.04​S2\texttt{init\_num}=0.04\,S^{2} and forms a square of side length side=2​⌊init_num⌋\texttt{side}=2\lfloor\sqrt{\texttt{init\_num}}\rfloor, placing agents on an every-other-cell lattice (stride 2) to avoid overlap. The two formations are separated by a horizontal gap of gap=3\texttt{gap}=3 cells centered around the midline.

Reference visualization.

Figure 4 shows a representative 6464 vs 6464 configuration.

A.2 Pursuit (pursuit_v3)

Scenario sizes.

In Pursuit, the world is a square grid of size S×SS\times S, where SS depends on the population scale (Table 4).

State and observations.

The environment maintains a 3-channel grid state consisting of: (i) static obstacles/walls, (ii) pursuer occupancy, and (iii) evader occupancy. Each pursuer observes a local R×RR\times R patch centered on itself with obs_range=R\texttt{obs\_range}=R (default R=7R=7), returned as a 3-channel tensor. Pursuers act in a discrete action space corresponding to primitive grid movements and a tag action.

Catching rule (surround).

We use surround=True\texttt{surround}=\texttt{True} throughout. An evader at location (x,y)(x,y) is removed when pursuers occupy all open 4-neighborhood cells (up/down/left/right) around (x,y)(x,y), and tag the evader. The number of required surrounding cells accounts for map boundaries and obstacles (i.e., fewer than 4 are required if some neighboring cells are blocked or out-of-bounds). Each pursuer that participates in a surround event is credited as a catcher.

Rewards and termination.

The default reward parameters are catch_reward=5.0\texttt{catch\_reward}=5.0 (awarded to catchers when an evader is removed), tag_reward=0.0\texttt{tag\_reward}=0.0, and urgency_reward=0.0\texttt{urgency\_reward}=0.0. So, this is a very sparse reward environment. An episode terminates when all evaders are removed or upon reaching the time limit max_cycles=500\texttt{max\_cycles}=500 steps.

Controlled team and opponent policy.

In all Pursuit experiments, we control the pursuers, while the evaders move randomly around the map.

Initialization.

At reset, pursuers and evaders are randomly initialized within a (possibly constrained) window of the map. In our runs we use constraint_window=1.0\texttt{constraint\_window}=1.0, which corresponds to sampling across the full map.

Reference visualization.

Figure 5 shows a representative 2020P–88E configuration.

Appendix B Hyperparameters and Architecture

This section provides a reproducibility-oriented summary of (i) model architectures, (ii) PPO optimization settings, and (iii) communication- and grouping-specific hyperparameters. Unless stated otherwise, the same settings are used across both benchmarks.

B.1 Model architecture

Actor.

Each agent uses a recurrent policy with GRU hidden size h=64h=64. At each environment step, the agent observation is first embedded with a linear layer and ReLU, then processed by a GRU:

obst→Linear+ReLUet∈ℝh→GRU​(h,h)ut∈ℝh.\text{obs}_{t}\xrightarrow{\text{Linear+ReLU}}e_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{h}\;\;\xrightarrow{\text{GRU}(h,h)}\;\;u_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{h}.

From utu_{t}, the actor outputs three heads: (i) environment action logits, (ii) a binary “send” decision logits, and (iii) recipient-selection logits over the NN candidate recipients.

Descriptor network.

A descriptor network encodes per-agent inputs into: (i) a grouping descriptor zgrp∈ℝ64z_{\text{grp}}\in\mathbb{R}^{64} used for soft group assignments, and (ii) a message feature zmsg∈ℝ96z_{\text{msg}}\in\mathbb{R}^{96} used as the content representation for communication and for the communication critic. Descriptor MLPs apply LayerNorm at the output, and observations use running normalization.

Mailbox aggregation (parameter-free attention).

Incoming messages are aggregated with a single-head dot-product attention in message-feature space: for each recipient, attention weights are a softmax over senders (scaled by 1/d1/\sqrt{d}), and the mailbox is the weighted sum of sender message vectors. All agents are eligible recipients.

Group-aware critic.

A group critic maps the global state to per-group values using a 2-layer MLP (ReLU, no layer normalization),

Vgrp:s→ℝh→ℝh→ℝM,V_{\text{grp}}:\;\;s\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{h}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{h}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{M},

and produces per-agent values via the (soft) group assignment matrix PτP_{\tau}.

Communication critic.

We use two small MLPs (ReLU, no layer normalization): (i) a value network V⁡(⋅)V(\cdot) that takes global state concatenated with an agent feature vector, and (ii) an edge-value network Q⁡(i→j)Q(i\!\to\!j) that takes global state concatenated with sender and recipient features. The agent feature includes zmsgz_{\text{msg}}, the incoming mailbox embedding, the send bit, and the MM-dimensional soft group assignment.

B.2 Optimization and training

PPO.

We use PPO with rollout length 2048 environment steps per update, 8 update epochs, minibatch size 4096, and clipping parameter ε=0.2\varepsilon=0.2. Discounting uses γ=0.99\gamma=0.99 and GAE uses λ=0.95\lambda=0.95. The value loss coefficient is 0.5 and the maximum gradient norm is 1.0. We use Adam with learning rate 3×10−43\times 10^{-4}. Entropy regularization coefficients are: environment action 0.02, send decision 0.01, and recipient selection 0.01.

Grouping objective and schedules.

Soft group assignments use a Gumbel–Softmax temperature schedule linearly annealed from τ=10\tau=10 to τ=0.5\tau=0.5 over training. Assignments are prototype-based using cosine similarity to MM learnable prototypes with logit scale 3.0. Auxiliary grouping losses use: balance weight 0.1, row-entropy weight 0.01, and an edge-utility weight linearly scheduled from 0 to 1 over training.

Macro-step.

Group assignments and the corresponding group-induced recipient prior are recomputed every K=10K=10 environment steps.

For convenience, Table 5 summarizes the shared architecture and training hyperparameters described above.

B.3 Benchmark-specific settings

Number of groups MM.

We set the number of groups using simple scale-dependent heuristics:

Battle:M=⌊N⌋,Pursuit:M=⌊E2⌋,\textbf{Battle:}\;\;M=\left\lfloor\sqrt{N}\right\rfloor,\qquad\textbf{Pursuit:}\;\;M=\left\lfloor\frac{E}{2}\right\rfloor,

where NN is the number of agents per team in Battle and EE is the number of evaders in Pursuit. Tables 6 and 7 list MM for the population scales reported in the main paper. The choice of these scale-dependent heuristics is further justified through a sensitivity study in Appendix D.

Appendix C Additional Results

We visualize rollout snapshots from a single illustrative evaluation episode of SCoUT at the headline scale for each benchmark: 100v100 Battle (map size 5050, pretrained opponents) and 100P–40E Pursuit. For each episode, we report four frames at progression timesteps t∈{0,⌊T/4⌋,⌊T/2⌋,T}t\in\{0,\lfloor T/4\rfloor,\lfloor T/2\rfloor,T\}, where TT is the final timestep of the shown episode. We also report a post-hoc in-group message fraction from the same setting to support the claim that the learned interaction structure concentrates communication within groups.

C.1 Battle (100v100)

Key events (Figure 6).

At t=0t=0, both teams begin in symmetric spawn regions. As contact occurs, SCoUT’s recipient selection becomes structured: messages are preferentially routed within the same (soft) group, which typically corresponds to nearby agents and locally coordinated attacks. By mid-episode, the controlled red agents form multiple coherent sub-engagements, rather than a single diffuse front. By the final frame, remaining red agents tend to appear in spatially coherent pockets, consistent with localized, group-driven coordination.

C.2 Pursuit (100P–40E)

Key events (Figure 7).

Initially, pursuers spread across the map and begin forming local coalitions around nearby evaders. As the episode progresses, subteams emerge that repeatedly execute surround-and-capture behaviors in different regions of the map (visible as clusters of pursuers tightening around evaders). This behavior is consistent with a group-induced recipient bias: communication emphasizes coordination among agents that are already acting as a local capture unit, reducing unnecessary cross-map broadcast.

C.3 Effect of grouping: in-group message fraction

To quantify whether communication aligns with the learned interaction structure, we compute the in-group message fraction: the fraction of realized sender–recipient message edges (i→j)(i\!\to\!j) for which sender and recipient belong to the same group. Concretely, at each macro-step we obtain soft assignments Pτ∈[0,1]N×MP_{\tau}\in[0,1]^{N\times M} and define a hard group label g^​(i)=arg⁡maxm​Pτ​(i,m)\hat{g}(i)=\arg\max_{m}P_{\tau}(i,m). Let ℰ\mathcal{E} denote the set of all realized sender-recipient message edges during an episode. We report

InGroupFrac=1|ℰ|∑(i→j)∈ℰ𝕀[g^(i)=g^(j)].\text{InGroupFrac}\;=\;\frac{1}{|\mathcal{E}|}\sum_{(i\to j)\in\mathcal{E}}\mathbb{I}\!\left[\hat{g}(i)=\hat{g}(j)\right].

We average this metric over 10 evaluation seeds. This is a diagnostic metric used only for analysis and is not itself optimized as a training objective. Table 8 reports the in-group fraction across all scales, together with the random baseline 1/M1/M.

Across all reported scales, the in-group message fraction is well above the 1/M1/M baseline, indicating that recipient selection is strongly aligned with the learned group structure. This supports the qualitative rollouts in Figure 6 and Figure 7 and is consistent with the role of grouping in SCoUT: it induces a slowly-varying interaction structure during training that reduces diffuse broadcast and promotes localized coordination.

Appendix D Sensitivity to Number of Groups and Macro-Step Length

SCoUT introduces two environment-facing hyperparameters that control the granularity and temporal persistence of the learned interaction structure: the number of groups MM and the macro-step length KK. This section evaluates how sensitive performance is to (M,K)(M,K), and whether the choice of K=10K{=}10 and scale-dependent MM, used in the main experiments, lies in a stable high-performing region.

Settings.

We perform controlled sweeps on two representative, computationally manageable scales: Pursuit 40P--16E and Battle 64v64. These settings are large enough to exhibit nontrivial coordination dynamics, while being substantially cheaper computationally than the largest stress-test cases. Even at these scales, each 4×44{\times}4 sweep required approximately 4 days per benchmark, making analogous sweeps at larger scales prohibitively expensive.

D.1 Experimental setup

Grid over (M,K)(M,K).

For each benchmark, we evaluate a 4×44\times 4 grid:

M∈{4,6,8,12},K∈{5,10,15,20}.M\in\{4,6,8,12\},\qquad K\in\{5,10,15,20\}.

The grid includes the default configuration used in the main paper, (M=8,K=10)(M{=}8,K{=}10), which corresponds to our scale rules at 64v64 Battle (M=⌊64⌋=8M=\lfloor\sqrt{64}\rfloor=8) and 40P--16E Pursuit (M=⌊16/2⌋=8M=\lfloor 16/2\rfloor=8).

Training protocol and metric.

All runs use identical hyperparameters except for (M,K)(M,K) (Appendix B) and are trained for 2000 iterations. We report the final average episode return for each configuration. Figures 8 and 9 visualize the resulting performance surfaces.

D.2 Results and interpretation

Battle 64v64.

Figure 8 shows a sharp dependence on MM. Very small MM performs poorly across KK, with M=4M{=}4 yielding the lowest returns for all KK. In contrast, intermediate group counts are substantially stronger: the best configuration is (M=8,K=10)(M{=}8,K{=}10), with nearby settings remaining competitive. For large MM, average reward remains positive but is typically below the best region. This pattern is consistent with the intuition that Battle benefits from meaningful group structure, while still retaining enough within-group mass to coordinate local engagements.

Pursuit 40P--16E.

Figure 9 shows a clear best-performing configuration at (M=8,K=10)(M{=}8,K{=}10). Furthemore, several settings also achieve competitive return: (M=6,K=15)(M{=}6,K{=}15) at 10.1810.18, (M=4,K=10)(M{=}4,K{=}10) at 10.1310.13, and (M=12,K=20)(M{=}12,K{=}20) at 10.0810.08). Overall, the sweep supports the default (8,10)(8,10) while indicating that SCoUT is less sensitive to the choice of (M,K)(M,K)in Pursuit as compared to Battle, which showed a more structured and sharper dependence on MM.

Takeaway.

Across both benchmarks, the sweeps place the best-performing region at or near the default choice (M=8,K=10)(M{=}8,K{=}10) used in the main experiments. The observed trends align with the roles of the two hyperparameters: MM controls interaction granularity—too small can reduce selectivity and induce broadcast-like communication; too large can fragment coalitions. On the other hand, KK controls persistence—too small can introduce unnecessary churn; too large can make the interaction structure stale in dynamic settings. Together, these results provide additional justification for using K=10K{=}10 with scale-dependent MM in the main paper without per-scale tuning.
